reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Read DRAFT, CONTEXT, SOURCE and the_change first; opened ADMISSION.json only after my own pass. CHANGE CHECK: the_change asks for Emulate's one sentence (sample cl) in place of the inner child guide's “Borrowed is fine, …”. The draft is one sentence, “Borrow some from someone else if you need to, but make sure they're stable and not someone who will try to direct your trip.”; CONTEXT holds it once, as the last sentence of the first paragraph of Appendix G, and the source sentence is gone. MEANING vs SOURCE: “Borrowed is fine” (the Nurturer and Protector of the sentence before, from someone else) becomes “Borrow some from someone else if you need to”; “as long as it’s from someone steady” becomes “but make sure they're stable”; “who won’t try to run your trip for you” becomes “and not someone who will try to direct your trip”. All three parts survive: borrowing is allowed, the lender must be steady, the lender must not take over the trip. Small shifts, none that adds a fact: “is fine” (permitted) becomes an imperative with “if you need to”, which only restates what the sentence before sets up (“enough Nurturer and Protector in the room”: if you don't have enough, borrow); “as long as” becomes “make sure”, the same condition said as a check; “run … for you” becomes “direct”, the same idea of taking over. No first person, no study, no figure. READS IN CONTEXT: it follows “I’d learn the inner child work sober first, with enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep (see the inner child reparenting section).” “Some” is the Nurturer and Protector of that sentence (“enough … some” pairs as a quantity of a mass noun) and “else” fits borrowing something you would normally supply yourself; “they're” is the someone else. This is the one spot I slowed down on: with “substances” and “use them” earlier in the paragraph and the cross-reference parenthetical sitting between, “borrow some” could for a moment be heard as borrowing the substance. I judge it resolves inside the paragraph (“sober first” just before, “if you need to”, “stable” and “direct your trip” all describe a person who sits with you, and a borrowed substance would contradict the paragraph's own opening disclaimer), and the source's “Borrowed is fine” leans on the same earlier sentence with less to anchor it, so the change is no worse than what it replaces. Noted for the author's eye, not a fail. “…they're stable and not someone who …” mixes an adjective with a negated noun phrase, but it is conversational. The straight apostrophe in “they're” matches several others in this appendix (“you've”, “you're”, “it's”), so no mismatch with the page. TELL ROWS: went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft inside its paragraph; none is PRESENT. Looked hardest at: T10 and T22 (“if you need to” is a permission phrase, but it is tied to the “enough Nurturer and Protector” just before, and the second half gives a reason and a safety rule, so it is not reassurance alone; the source's “is fine” was the more coach-like of the two); T12 and T21 (stable and not-controlling are the two ways a borrowed helper can go wrong, both are needed, and the source already had both in one sentence); T15 (steady to stable and run to direct are common words, not less likely ones, and the sentence is restructured, not just re-worded); T16 and T18 (no “not X, it's Y” flip, and the “but” adds a condition, it does not knock a premise down); T20 and T29 (it ends the paragraph on a new condition, not a summary or a clever closer); T26 (“someone” twice in one sentence is plain speech). C01 not named “the kid”; C02 as above, “some” and “they're” point where they should; C03 and C04 none. LINTER FINDINGS: “D9 follows the source order” – accepted: one sentence swapped for one sentence, so it follows the source's order by construction and moves nothing (T14 absent); the T13 and T09 check it asks for finds a real risk noticed in passing (a helper who takes over) and nothing equalized. “E36/E41 heavy second person” (8.3 per 100) – accepted: that is 2 of 24 words (“you need to”, “your trip”) in one short caution, inside an appendix addressed to “you” throughout, and the sentence is a safety condition, not coaching. INDEPENDENCE NOTE: my context also held the repository's standing instruction files, which the harness loads automatically; I saw none of the writer's reasoning beyond ADMISSION.json, which I opened after forming my own rows, and I agree with its rows and its two linter dispositions.
